extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of classical Euclidean geometry (learners/scholars of Euclid's Elements)
extracted.subtask_description: Extraction of geometric propositions, constructions, and definitions (Euclid Book I style) appearing in the page: classical statements about triangle construction, congruence, parallel lines, similarity, Pythagorean relation, and related constructions. Intended for use in geometric reasoning or discussion on Math StackExchange.

rubrics_metrics.name: Construction of a triangle from three given straight lines
rubrics_metrics.description: Given three straight lines, construct a triangle whose sides are equal respectively to the three given straight lines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text describes taking one of the given segments as a base, then with centers at the base endpoints describing circles with radii equal to the other two given segments; the intersection of the circles gives the third vertex and thus the triangle (use of circle intersections to construct triangle from three sides).

rubrics_metrics.name: Copy (construct) an angle equal to a given angle at a given point on a given line
rubrics_metrics.description: Given a straight line and a point on it (or its extension) and a given angle, to construct at that point an angle equal to the given angle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Procedure uses equal arcs and equal chord segments: mark equal distances along rays from the given angle, transfer those distances along the given line using circles, then join intersections to replicate the angle. (Classic Euclidean angle-copy construction.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Side–Angle–Side congruence (SAS)
rubrics_metrics.description: If two triangles have two sides of the one equal to two sides of the other respectively, and have the angles contained by those sides equal, then the triangles are equal (congruent).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page states this congruence criterion and uses it to deduce equality of bases and other corresponding parts; this is used repeatedly to prove further propositions and to construct equal triangles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Isosceles triangle base angles equality (and converse)
rubrics_metrics.description: If two sides of a triangle are equal, then the base angles are equal; conversely, if the base angles are equal then the sides are equal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The classical Euclidean statement appears: equal sides imply equal opposite angles and vice versa; the text uses constructions and equal triangles to demonstrate both directions.

rubrics_metrics.name: If a straight line cutting two lines makes alternate interior angles equal then the lines are parallel (and converses)
rubrics_metrics.description: A straight line falling across two straight lines makes the alternate angles equal if and only if the two lines are parallel. Similarly, corresponding equal angles or interior angles on the same side summing to two right angles characterize parallel lines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Multiple equivalent formulations are given: alternate interior angles equal ⇒ lines equidistant/parallel; corresponding angles equal ⇒ parallel; interior angles on same side summing to two right angles ⇒ parallel. These are used to identify or construct parallel lines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Through a given point draw a line parallel to a given line (parallel construction)
rubrics_metrics.description: Given a line and a point not on it, construct a straight line through the point parallel to the given line.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construction is achieved by copying corresponding angles (or using the alternate/corresponding angle criterion): reproduce the required angle at the given point so that a line through the point makes the same angle with a transversal, yielding a parallel line.

rubrics_metrics.name: Triangles equiangular are similar; proportional sides follow
rubrics_metrics.description: If two triangles have their angles equal (are equiangular), then the sides about the equal angles are proportional and the triangles are similar.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page contains definitions and propositions relating angle equality to proportionality of corresponding sides and similarity of figures; these are used to relate triangles and larger polygon decompositions (e.g., reducing polygons to triangles to compare areas/proportions).

rubrics_metrics.name: If corresponding sides of two triangles are proportional, triangles are similar
rubrics_metrics.description: If in two triangles the sides about two angles are proportionally equal (or all three sides are proportional), then the triangles have corresponding angles equal and hence are similar.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the converse similarity criterion: proportionality of sides implies equality of corresponding angles; the text discusses proportionality and multiplicative relationships among sides when proving similarity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Construction of a figure equal (in area) to a given triangle (e.g., a square equal to a given triangle)
rubrics_metrics.description: Given a triangle, construct a square (or other polygonal figure) equal in area to that triangle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page outlines procedures to convert a triangle into an equal-area quadrilateral or square by decomposing into triangles, using equal parallels and equal-area parallelograms, and classical Euclidean area-transfer constructions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pythagorean relation (square on hypotenuse equals sum of squares on other two sides)
rubrics_metrics.description: In a right-angled triangle, the square on the side opposite the right angle (hypotenuse) is equal to the sum of the squares on the sides that contain the right angle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text explicitly states and gives reasoning for: in a right triangle the square on the hypotenuse equals the two squares on the other sides. It also discusses constructions of squares on sides and relations among them (Euclid I.47/Prop. 47).

rubrics_metrics.name: Construction/description of gnomon and relations of gnomon with squares/parallelograms
rubrics_metrics.description: Statements about forming gnomons (figures formed by subtracting a rectangle/square from a larger square) and the relationships of such complements to given squares/parallelograms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page uses the notion of gnomon and successive additions/subtractions of squares and parallelograms (e.g., adding a 'gnomon' to a square equals certain other figures) in area arguments; these are Euclidean constructions used in area equalities and multiplication analogues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Properties and construction of parallelograms and complements (parallelogram-related equalities)
rubrics_metrics.description: Propositions about parallelograms: equal parallelograms on the same base and between the same parallels are equal in area; complements and supplements about a diameter produce equal figures; parallel lines produce proportional/ equal segments, etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text treats parallels, diameters, and the parallelogram decomposition into supplementary parallelograms; it states how parallel strips around a diameter form equal areas and how supplementary parallelograms are equal when appropriately constructed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition and properties of similar figures (polygons) via triangle decomposition
rubrics_metrics.description: Two plane figures are similar when their angles are equal respectively and the ratios of the sides containing equal angles are proportionally equal; many propositions reduce general polygon similarity to similarity of constituent triangles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page repeatedly reduces polygonal similarity questions to triangles: divide polygons into triangles by diagonals, compare corresponding triangle proportions and angles, and then deduce similarity or area proportions of the whole figures.

rubrics_metrics.name: If many lines are proportionally placed, corresponding constructed figures are similar and proportional
rubrics_metrics.description: If a set of lines are in proportion to another set (e.g., multiple proportional segments along diagonals or bases), then the figures built on those proportional lines (triangles, pentagons, etc.) will be similar in corresponding fashion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Text explains that if first set of lines are proportional to another set, the figures constructed from the first set correspond and are similar to the ones from the second set; used to assemble complex polygons from triangular pieces with proportional sides.
